If my hon. friend is fair he will admit that these reductions have been made in controllable expenditure; for of course as he knows there are certain expenditures that are not controllable.

The Public
Works expenditure on current account is reduced, it is true, eleven millions below the Estimates of last year, but there are still thirty-two million dollars-

I am not stating
what they were last year; what I am pointing out is that on the first opportunity to reduce expenditure this Government has had since the war, it has reduced expenditure to the large amount of over $17,000,000 on controllable items in connection with the departments which my hon. friend attacked.
You have reduced the whole lot $10,000,000, whereas the reduction should have been thirty or forty million dollars.

The total reduction
is $17,780,320, which is a pretty respectable cutting down at one stroke. I believe, Sir, that public opinion has endorsed this Budget to the full extent. The proposed taxation falls upon financial institutions and those who are able to bear the taxes. The revenue had to be _ raised, and the question confronting the Government	was	how	it could	be raisedin	the	most desirable	manner.The proposed taxation does not fall on the farmer or on. the workingman, and both these classes are throughly satisfied with the Budget as it stands at present. They ought to be satisfied. Hon. members	who	came	from rural	communities	can	speak	as to the	farmers;
but I can speak as to the men in

the cities, and they are thoroughly satisfied, because they realize that these taxes which are very necessary have been imposed very generally, principally upon the moneyed interests, and that they have not affected the artisan or workman except in a very minor respect.
My hon. friend cavils at protection. Protection seems to be the red rag that angers Liberals in this House and out of it. I have no apology to make for protection; l am a stalwart protectionist. Protection has built up Canada. When this country is in straitened circumstances, as it will he more or less, and as all other countries will be owing to the war, and after it is over, it will be protection and the protectionist interests and the * National Policy over again that will rebuild this country and put it back where it was before the outbreak of the war, and make it even more prosperous than ever before. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Michael Clark) is perhaps amused at that statement, but history will prove that it is the truth.
This afternoon I asked my hon. friend from Halifax a question which he did not answer. He was deprecating the immense amount of money spent on the Civil Service. I asked him if he would be in favour of a reduction of ten per cent in the salaries of all employees.

If the service
had not been improperly increased, the amount spent on it would have been more than ten per cent below what it is.

I will answer that
in this way. My hon. friend made a point of attacking the Customs Department. If he will take the revenue collected and the expense of collecting that revenue he will find that the percentage of expense for collection is not any greater to-day than it was five or ten years ago.
What will it be in 1914-15?
I hope it will be high, because that will mean a big revenue.

But the percentage of
revenue?
. Mr. MACDONELL:	I am not guessing;
I am just trying to give facts.
It will be over five per cent.

The Government are to be congratulated also on the arrange-244
ments they have made for their war borrowings. They have made arrangements to borrow all the money necessary for war purposes. Let me be reminiscent with regard to our borrowings. On the first of October, 1913, we paid off the last of the old Imperial guaranteed loan amounting to $8,273,333. This was the last loan which Canada had bearing the underwriting of the British Government guaranteeing it in the markets of the world. In 1869 there was $7,300,000 of an Imperial guaranteed loan outstanding. In 1874 it stood at $16,000,000. In 1885 it stood at $31,600,000, part of which was used to purchase Rupert's Land which made a Canadian nation possible, part for the defence of the country, part for public works, and so on. The last of that loan,	as I said, was paid off a
short	time	ago.	To-day we find
history repeating itself, but in a better way. Canada is borrowing to-day not by British guarantees, because the loan for which the Government have arranged is one made jointly with Great Britain. Canada is participating in that loan and in its advantages equally with Great Britain. Canada is getting the same terms as Great Britain, though no longer in the position of having Great Britain's guarantee. Great Britain is borrowing with Canada, and Canada is borrowing with Great Britain. It is to all intents and purposes a partnership; and on both sides of the House it is a matter of congratulation that Canada has lived through the early stages of her history with Great Britain standing behind her, and that now Canada is standing by Great Britain and Great Britain is standing by Canada, and Canada will stand by Great Britain to the end of this war and I trust to the end of time.
Notwithstanding our borrowings, the Budget makes out a strong case for a large amount of increased taxation. The situation must be faced. To temporize would be weak from a financial standpoint. The situation has to be grasped with a strong hand. The Government have presented a determined front to every phase of the war situation which has appeared. They have mastered the mobilization of the troops and have co-operated with Great Britain as regards our loans and other matters of importance connected with financing the war. Our trade has been protected by Government action as far as possible; our banking has been safeguarded and made permanent and strong, and quite recently the Government have provided seed grain and other assistance

for the farmers in the West who are in need, so that they in turn may be able to reap a large harvest and bear their share of the war taxation when the proper time comes. Although the fact is not pleasing to my hon. friend from Halifax, the Government are proceeding with the construction of public works. My hon. friend comes from a city. Does he think it would be wise or proper to discontinue in an hour all the public works in the cities in Canada? Surely not. Private individuals look to the Government for an example. They want to see a strong Government going on with its work, undertaking and facing its obligations; and the business men and capitalists throughout Canada are doing their share to prevent unemployment. They are giving employment to men whenever it can be secured; and wherever it cannot be secured, they are putting the men on short time and are treating them as humanely as existing conditions will permit. In that the Government is taking its share and it is right that it should do so. The Government is strong and Canada is strong, notwithstanding what we see in the Toronto Globe-because we all read the Globe; even gentlemen on this side of toe House read the Globe. I see by that paper that we are in for a "smash." In an editorial it tells us that the smash has actually arrived-Canada smashed, industry and enterprise smashed. It is a nice object lesson to Germany and the other continental nations whom we are fighting to be told by a paper of the prominence and eminence of the Globe that Canada is smashed.
A bad moral.

That is not a desirable thing to say, and the statement is absolutely without foundation and is also very silly.
My hon. friend from Halifax spoke rather emphatically about there being no necessity for a revenue Budget. I presume he is aware of the fact that for the first ten months of the present fiscal year the revenue from Customs has fallen off $28,000,000, and that the estimated falling off for the whole year is $33,000,000. I am reminded by an hon. gentleman that the hon. junior member for Halifax rejoices in that fact.
Not at all.

My hon. friend says that there has apparently been no loss to Canada or to the Government by the interruption of trade and ocean traffic. My hon. friend surely knows better than that.
[ Mr. Macdonell.]
The falling off is due in a great measure to the use by the British Government of a great number of ships for the transport of soldiers and so on. Practically all ocean freight traffic has been tied up or ruined because there are not sufficient ships for the Canadian trade. My hon. friend comes from a maritime district, and knows that fact very well. It is no news to any one. The hon. gentleman has admitted that because of the war this country has not received a large addition to its finances. I am glau he makes that assertion; it simply corroborates what the Minister of Finance said as to the condition in which the country finds itself as a result of the war. My hon. friend is probably aware of the fact that borrowing in England is now prohibited by Royal proclamation; English investors of money cannot lend in the British Dominions without the consent of the Treasury Board. This circumstance operates greatly to decrease the flow of money into Canada, thus affecting not only the industries of the country, but the Government as well.
Is th; t not a good reason why the Government should cut down expenditures?
It is a good reason why trade has been almost ruined through the commercial congestion and depression which has been the result of lack of money.

I would remind the hon. member that the Minister of Finance estimated that for 1915-16, with the taxation now in force, he could get a revenue of $120,000,000, only $10,000,000 below the amount he will receive for the present fiscal year.
What does that establish?
If you have a revenue of $120,000,000, why do you not cut down your expenditures?

I have given the reasons why certain expenditures have been cut down, and I am endeavouring to give reasons why it is not possible to cut down everything. You cannot cut all expenditures down; my hon. friend knows that.
My hon. friend denies that this is a war tax, but I submit that this a war tax, if there ever was one. They are made necessary by the war, whether the proceeds are used to buy guns and war material or to make good revenue deficits caused by dislocation of trade and consequent loss of revenue. The war has closed off borrowing

by Canadian corporations, thereby diminishing imports.
The new taxes will pay interest on- war loans, pensions, and part of capital expenditure. The interest on the $50,000,000 to be borrowed this year and the $100,000,(LO to be borrowed next year will amount to nearly $7,500,000 annually. This the new taxes will have to provide for, together with interest on additional borrowings during the war. It must also provide for a pension list amounting to about $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 a year. If there were no war the Government could borrow money in the London market under the usual conditions, but, as I have attempted to show, the war makes that impossible.
Hon. gentlemen opposite take issue with, the Government with regard to these taxes, being war taxes. Hon. gentlemen opposite, especially the hon. member for Halifax (Mr..Maclean), have been wont in times gone by to cast eyes across tne border when looking for precedents and encouragement. What has happened in the United States, a neutral country, which is not embroiled in this war? Although they have no hand m the quarrel;' although they are simply bystandees, they have been affected to such an extent by the war conditions that they have experienced a very great decrease in revenue. Qn September 4, last, in making an address to Congress asking them to pass a war tax bill, President Wilson said:
During the month of August there was as compared with the corresponding month of last year, a falling off of $10,629,538 in the revenues collected from customs. A continuation of this decrease in the same proportion throughout the current fiscal year would probably mean a loss oi customs revenues from sixty to one hundred millions. I need not tell you to what this falling off is due. It is due, in chief part, not to the reductions recently made in the customs duties, but to the great decrease in importations ; and that is due to the extraordinary extent of the industrial area affected by the present war in Europe. Conditions have arisen which no man foresaw; they affect the whole world of commerce and economic production; and they must be faced and dealt with.
How did Congress face and deal with that message? They passed Bill No. 217 of the 63rd Congress, entitled an Act to increase the internal revenue and for other purposes. I wish to read one or two extracts from the report of the committee to which that Bill, together with the address of the President, was referred for report.
The Committee of Ways and Means, to whom was referred House Bill H. R. 18891, to increase the internal revenue, and for other purposes, having had the same under consideration, report it back to the House, with certain minor amendments.	,
Then follows, under the heading, " Necessity of this Legislation ":
The necessity for this legislation grows out of the reduction of revenue derived from customs receipts caused by the disturbed conditions resulting from the war in Europe.
The following table shows the value of the dutiable imports into the United States from the European countries at war during the fiscal year ending June, 1914, together with the estimated falling off in customs revenue during the next 12 months, computed on the basis of Tariff Act of October 3, 1913.
Then follows a table showing the estimated falling off in revenue during the next twelve months, which is totalled at $125,811,000. On the next page I find the following:
The necessity for this legislation cannot be traced to the Tariff Act of 1913. If it had not been for the war in Europe the Tariff Act of October 3, 1913 and the other sources of revenue would have yielded sufficient revenue to meet the demands of the Government.
Under the heading "Effects of the European War" is the following:
The countries now at war comprise Austria-Hungary, Belgium, France, Germany, Japan, Russia, Servia, Montenegro and the United Kingdom of Great Britain. If it were not for remained the same as those of last year; had remain the same as those of last year, the customs taxes levied by the present tariff Act from said countries would have yielded $133,079,000. This does not include the importation from other countries that will naturally bring the customs devenue that is directly affected by war conditions to an amount over $150,000,000. The fact that the ships of these belligerent countries carried over 80 per cent of the foreign commerce entering our ports and the further fact that war conditions have disturbed the lines of transportation belonging to these countries and forced many of their tramp steamers to remain in port, will seriously affect the importation of merchandise coming from neutral countries, and thereby cause a diminution of customs revenues from-neutral as well as belligerent countries.
It, therefore, seems to be the part of wisdom for the Congress to levy a tax at this time to take care of the deficit in our customs revenues brought about by conditions over which our Government and our people have no control.
Is that not -an exact parallel of the conditions existing here to-day? A non-belligerent-neutral country, situated as we are and subject to the same commercial conditions, saw fit to pass an act of this kind long before we introduced our legislation, and for the same-reasons. '	'
The proposed tariff changes do not, I submit, mean more protection. My hon. friend; as are all gentlemen opposite, is subject to the protection bogey. The ihcreased tariff, as my hon. friend knows, applies to raw materials, so that when raw materials come, into this country to be used in the mami-

facture of various commodities, duties will be paid upon them. My hon. friend spoke particularly to-day about wool and cotton. If they come in, as I hope they will, in abundant quantities, to be manufactured by the workmen of Canada and sold to our own people or Shipped, abroad, a duty will be paid on the raw material and there will be a compensation in that respect.
That will be an offset to any additional duty placed upon manufactured goods that may come from other countries.
My hon. friend is fearful for the British preference. The British preference is greater than it was before; the British manufacturer is better off; he gains 24 per cent as compared with his foreign competitor. Take an article which under the old general tariff paid 30 per cent and under the preferential 20 per cent. Add 7J per cent to the general duty and you have 374 per cent; add 5 per cent to the British preferential duty and you have 25 per cent; therefore you have a preference of 124 per cent whereas before the preference it was 10 per cent. So the British shipper is better off than he was by 2J per cent. Why this wail about the British manufacturer? Why this grief and fear on account of the British exporter to our country? He is better off than he was before, especially-
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends
laugh-as compared with the foreign competitor of course.

You increase the duty
and make him better off.

Certainly, as compared with his foreign competitor. There is no doubt about that. If the general tariff had been increased and there had been no increase in the duty under the Imperial preference Canadian industries would have been ruined. Let us bear that in mind. If you increased the general tariff by 74 per cent or 104 per cent or 204 per cent and made no increase in the duty under the British preferential tariff, you would ruin the Canadian manufacturer; and for my part I adopt with the greatest possible enthusiasm the statement made by the hon. leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) on more than one occasion, in this House and out of it, both before and after the change of Government, that an industry in any Canadian city is as good for the Empire as an industry in Birmingham or any other British city-and much better for Canada. Surely the very essence of our relationship with the Old Country is the

freedom and liberty which Great Britain allows always. We can compete with her if we want to, but we want to buin* up the Empire as a whole, and an industry in Toronto or Winnipeg is as great a factor in building up the Empire as one in Liverpool or Manchester. England builds up her trade and commerce; she is building up her greatness on the islands of Great Britain, and we are building up her greatness overseas in our own time and in our own way and in our own name. Our friends are still fearful of the bogey of protection. They did nothing to reduce the tariff when they had the power to do so. They allow themselves that delightful liberty and freedom, that splendid isolation in this case, of being able to blow hot and cold, of standing first on one foot and then on the other. One gentleman advocates one policy and another gentleman another, and the whole party advocate one policy in one province and another policy in another province. There is no consistency about the party on any subject; and so it is with protection. They could have reduced protection if they had desired to do so, if they thought it too high when they came into power. When they assumed office in 1896, the average rate of duty was 29-79 per cent; in 1911, when the change of Government took place, tb,e percentage was 26-71 per cent; so there was a reduction of about 3 per cent, notwithstanding the fact that the average price of merchandise had increased between those two dates by from 30 per cent to 40 per cent. So I do not see any merit now in the hon. gentlemen beating their breasts and tearing out their hair and shrieking against protection.
Then, as to spending money, our friend of the Globe got funny the other morning.
I do not know where the reverend editor was the night before, but he said that the Government was spending money like a drunken sailor. Let me give the foundation for Mr. Globeman's talk about spending money like a drunken sailor. He makes the statement that during the three years the Conservative party have been in power they have been spending money in a reckless manner, like a drunken sailor. I do not wish to go back to ancient history; some of us are still young men, and we do not need to take figures one hundred years old. Let us take the three years before and immediately after the great victory of the people of September 21, 1911, and what do we find as a result in regard to the expenditure of money? The years 1909, 1910 and 1911 show a net increase in the public debt of $62,000,000, while the three years

1912, 1913 and 1914 show a decrease in the public debt of $6,750,000, and this notwithstanding the fact that in these three latter years the Government expended large sums of money, aggregating about $130,000,000, on capital account, which moneys were taken from consolidated revenue fund account.
What is the record of surpluses for the same three years? That is a test, which my hon. friend from Halifax tried to apply this afternoon. The surplus in consolidated account for the year 1912 amounted to $37,946,000 ; for 1913 it amounted to $56,960,000, and for 1914, $35,000,000, a total surplus of $129,576,000 for the three years.
My hon. friends say that the Government may have saved money in one pocket but paid it out of the other. The country has only one pocket as a matter of fact, only one chest of money; but I will answer even the argument they make, if it be an argument. The large expenditure during the last three years was due to the fact that the Government inherited obligations and debts from the old Government which they had to pay, with respect to public works and undertakings and contracts entered into, such as the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Quebec bridge, the purchase of Grand Trunk Pacific bonds to the extent of $23,000,000, the loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific of $8,000,000, besides railway subsidies authorized by the late Government. Let me give an instance.
Halifax was referred to this afternoon. Coming west, let us take the great harbour of Quebec. I am making a statement of facts and not an argument. I want it to be understood that this Government had been committed to make expenditures that they could not disregard. I am not quoting these figures for the purpose of getting hot justice from the electors of Quebec at the next election. The expenditures on Quebec harbour since the present Government came into power in 1911 up to date, that is, for three years, as compared with the expenditures made by the Liberal party during the whole fourteen years of their term of office, were as follows: By the present Government, during their three years, $8,841,379; by the late Government, for the same period of time, $3,338,307. The present Government spent $8,000,000 and the late Government $3,000,000. Why did the present Government spend the $8,000,000? On account of the National Transcontinental railway, on account of the Quebec Harbour Commission, and on account of the Public Works Department. The late Government built a railway to Quebec and left it. How could the railway operate without terminals
and facilities of that kind? It had to have these or the whole road would have been wasted and all expenditure lost. That is why they have had to spend money, and they have done it.
That brings me to the question of railway subsidies. My hon. friend talked about subsidies, and they have been spoken of in the press. It has been said that these subsidies were a bugaboo, a very dreadful thing. I want to face that condition and tell the House the facts. There has been a substantial increase in the last three years in railway subsidies, which accounts for an annual expenditure of over $10,000,000 in that period. Over $2,000,000 a year was authorized by Acts of the late Government, and over $6,000,000 a year has gone to the Canadian Northern railway and its constituents on account of the old Government's guarantee of its bonds for upwards of $56,000,000. The Canadian Northern railway also got guarantees from the provinces to the extent of $76,000,000. This $76,000,000 and the $56,000,000 guaranteed by the Dominion were contingent liabilities. The time came when this road had to have more money and the cash subsidy which this Government is paying at the rate of over $6,000,000 a year was granted to prevent the guarantees which had already been given from becoming actual liabilities. Those are the facts. If this Government had not given the road that cash subsidy, the contingent liabilities of $76,000,000 by the provinces and $56,000,000 by this Government would have become actual liabilities, and the country and the provinces would have been called upon to pay them. That seems to me a very substantial reason why the Government should have given the subsidy. So that when you take the $6,000,000 and the $2,000,000, that means that this Government have only granted a $2,000,000 guarantee a year or thereabouts, since they have been in office for railway subsidies.
My hon. friend this afternoon dwelt ad nauseam I was going to say, but I will say very extensively, on the net debt. We had not been three years in office when war broke out and dislocated all trade. Our predecessors had fifteen years of office, and let us now compare the net debt of Canada as left by our predecessors with what it is now. In 1896 the net debt was $258,497,000, and in 1911 $340,042,000. That is, in those fifteen years the net debt was increased by $81,500,000, or at the comfortable rate of $5,000,000 a year. I am not objecting to a Government's spending money

properly, nor do I suggest that the money was wrongly spent, but the facts are obvious and what is the use of shutting our eyes to facts and doing the ostrich act like my hon. friend from Halifax did this afternoon. I am not criticising hon. gentlemen opposite for increasing the debt by that amount, but I say it is idle for them to turn around now and criticise the present Government for not having greatly reduced the net debt. Now look at the figures of the present Government. On the 31st March, 1914, the net debt was $333,300,000, and on the 31st March, 1911, $340,050,000. Whereas the previous Government had increased the debt by $81,500,000 in fifteen years, the present Government reduced the debt by $6,750,000 in three years. These are facts, and we know that the old adage says that facts are stubborn things. They cannot be got out of the way by such arguments as my hon. friend from Halifax used this afternoon.
In addition to that, this Government since it has been in power has spent nearly $130,000,000 of money taken from the current revenues and applied and used it for capital expenditure. The estimated taxation for 1910-11 was $89,350,000 as against $27,700,000 in 1896, when hon. gentlemen opposite took office; or $11.50 per head of population in 1910 as compared with $5.40 in 1896. In other words the late Government increased the debt on the people of this country from $5.40 per head to $11.50 per head between 1896 and 1911. I am not quoting these figures in the tu quoque manner, but it is not fair to criticise this Government for increasing the debt of Canada when, if any odium should be attached on account of that increase, it does and should rest on hon. gentlemen opposite.
I have already referred to the large expenditures this Government has made on account of contracts which had already been entered into. Large sums had been invested in public works throughout the country, and unless money had been supplied to continue those works they would simply have remained in a dormant state or rotted away. Would hon. gentlemen opposite prefer to see these public works which had cost tens of millions of dollars, rotting away rather than to spend the amount necessary to complete them. The necessity of giving employment to people of this country had also to be considered. The Government must set an example in this respect, and if I have any criticism to offer it is that the Government have been too stingy in carrying on the public works of this country

under the present conditions. But certainly they should not be blamed for having increased the expenditure.
Our borrowing for war purposes will be enormous, but our credit is first-class as the public accounts will show. We must keep up the credit of Canada. We have built up Canadian credit, and that is why Canada can bear the strain to-day.
I have already referred to the large increase in the volume of trade which this country is annually transacting. This has made necessary a large increase in the public service and an increase in the expenditure of that service. I have here the figures showing the total trade of Canada with all countries for a few years past. In 1908 the aggregate trade was $650,793,000; in 1909, $571,268,000; in 1910, $693,211,000; in 191l' $769,443,000; in 1912, $874,637,000; in 1913,' $1,085,264,000; in 1914, $1,129,744,000. The trade in merchandise only for the nine months ending 31st December, 1914, is estimated at $744,000,000. Increase in trade and revenue means an increase in the cost of collection, customs expenses and so on. If the Customs Department is collecting twice the revenue it did some years ago, it needs a larger staff. Surely that does not need to be laboured. I maintain that the increase in the gross expenditure by this Government was under the conditions proper and unavoidable, and as I have said, great expense has been incurred in carrying to completion the undertakings entered into by the old Government. Take the Department of Railways and Canals.. Comparing the three years previous to March 31, 1912, with the succeeding three years, we have an average annual expenditure during the first period of $37,426,000 as compared with $41,489,000 in the latter period, and having regard to the very great increase done by the Department of Railways and Canals I do not think the increase a large one. The average yearly earnings of Government railways should also be considered. The average yearly earnings of the Government railways during the respective three-year periods were $10,208,000 and $12,698,000; that is the average yearly earnings during the last three years under the old Government amounted to $10,208,000 and under the present Government they had reached $12,698,000. That, together with the increases in wages of employees, accounted for the increase in the revenue expenditures. Income expenditure shows an increase of $71,000 a year in the different departments, and the capital expenditure

shows an increase of $663,000 per year, which increase is accounted for by the expenditures upon the National Transcontinental railway, the Quebec bridge, the Hudson Bay railway, the Government railway, Canadian Government railways, the Welland ship canal and the Trent canal. All of these works were authorized by the old Government, with the sole exception of the Welland ship canal, the Halifax terminals and the Prince Edward Island car ferry. The Welland canal was endorsed by hon. gentlemen opposite, and we have yet to hear any complaints from them in regard to the Halifax terminals. That being our position, it seems to me that it is the duty of the Government to make the best of the present situation, to stand by the country, and to exercise every possible influence and energy that the country possesses, individually and collectively, for the purpose of tiding us over the trying time and permitting Canada when the war is over to take its stand again as the senior member of the great overseas dominions of the British Empire.
What is to be done by the Government, by public men, and by the industrial and business men of this country? I have just taken a glance at the exports from Germany, and I find that they have been very large. The trade of Germany, Austria-Hungary and the other enemy nations has been destroyed as far as the British Empire is concerned. Last year Germany exported to different countries throughout the world goods to the amount of $2,402,967,000, and that trade is at large to-day. Any one can get it who can take it. A great part of that trade belongs to the enterprising people who can compete in the markets of the world which have hitherto been supplied by Germany, and I believe there is no part of the world that can compete for that trade in a more effective and able manner than the people of Canada. Let us go after the chance. Great Britain was the largest consumer of German goods in the world; in fact, she was a greater consumer of German goods than any other two countries put together. Last year Germany exported to Canada and other overseas British dominions no less than $50,000,000 worth of goods. There is no part of the Empire that is better equipped in point of natural resources, raw material and energy of men to secure that trade than Canada. Twenty million dollars worth of that trade is our own. The total volume of the trade that Germany has hitherto done with Canada amounts to about $20,000,000 a
year. But there is $50,000,000 at large for the British Empire to secure. We have a preference in all overseas British dominions with the exception of Australia, and therefore we should he able to capture two-thirds of that trade. As I say, we have a preference in all the markets of the overseas dominions except that of Australia, and as we are the premier manufacturing overseas dominion of the Empire, outside of Great Britain herself, we have a splendid opportunity of capturing that $50,000,000 worth of trade. Let us make the best of it.
I am going to refer for a moment to a matter and this time with the approval of my friend the Globe. I see that the Globe has been advocating that the country engage in a propaganda of industrial research. That is not a new idea; in fact, it is an old idea in Canada, and it is older still in
9 p.m. other countries. The idea is to invoice the aid and assistance of our . universities and great seats of learning and knowledge and to send out to the world practical scientific men equipped with expert knowledge, to secure information in regard to manufacturing processes! and to ascertain the location of markets, etc., with reference particularly to those products the supply of which hitherto has been in the hands of Germany and which is now available to any one who may be able to capture it. Let me point out that in the University of Toronto they are now making anti-toxine for the relief of persons afflicted by diphtheria. It is a purely philanthropic work that is being done by university graduates and is the beginning of what I trust will be a very large public enterprise in the near future. They are also manufacturing tetanus, an anti-toxine for the use of the Red Cross Society for the treatment of lock-jaw and illnesses of that kind. The university, on the first small order saved the Red Cross Society no less than $3,000. We have many opportunities of securing the business that has been thrown open by the dislocation of the trade which Germany formerly did with Canada and the rest of the world.	-
All of which means that Canada will have either to supply herself from abroad with what she has heretofore purchased from enemy countries, or make it herself, which is the preferable course to adopt.
We must ascertain the entire quality and quantity of the products that we will require under the new conditions, so that we may supply ourselves with all these goods from this time forward, which means aggressive industrial research, so as to submit to capital

The Finance Minister, who presented the Budget, as well as my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Madem.), who criticised it on behalf of the Opposition, have both spoken of it as an extraordinary Budget, and as being excusable on the ground of extraordinary circumstances. 1 will agree that the circumstances are extraordinary and that the Budget is extraorumary. I will admit that

379 [DOT]
extraordinary circumstances would justify an extraordinary Budget, but I do not admit that the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance is a Budget that is adapted or auequate to the extraordinary circumstances which now have to be faced. My criticism would be, that notwithstanding the fact that the Finance Minister has introduced a new principle into the taxation of the country, there is still evidence both in the items of the Budget and in the arguments which have been made in support of it, that the Government itself does not realize the gravity of the present situation, either in regard to the financial condition of the Dominion or in regard to the duty of Canada as a part of the Empire in this present time of stress and trial. There has been criticism of the Budget on the ground that it does not recognize the changed financial conditions of the country by a reduction in the proposed expenditure, a point which has already been dealt with. But it is surely elementary, if our revenues are declining, and if there is no other prospect than that they will continue'to decline for an indefinite period, that it is the part of wisdom to introduce measures of economy of a substantial nature. That is a point that does not seem to have been considered by the Government as being of importance. My hon. friend (Mr. A. C. Macdonell), and I believe the Prime Minister as well, when this point was being dealt with, satisfied themselves and their friends by asking the member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in what particular he would reduce the expenditure, and especially if he would be willing to reduce the expenditure at the port of Halifax. I can only say that however satisfactory that form of answer may have been to the Prime Minister and to the hon. member, I do not think it will be satisfactory to the people of Canada. It is the gentlemen who occupy the Treasury benches and their friends behind them who are responsible for the disposition of the public moneys. They are answerable to the people for what use is made of these moneys, and it is for them to say when ana where and how moneys shall be spent, and to submit to criticism if money is spent for which provision has not been made, or for which no provision is intended to be made, so far as the Budget discloses.
I do not intend to weary the House with figures; but there is a point which has struck me in regard to the question of revenue and expenditure, of debt and deficit, that I will try to place before the
House at this time. I gather from the speech of the Minister of Finance that in the current fiscal year there will be added to the public debt the sum of $60,000,000, not including moneys borrowed on account sf the war. That increase of debt occurs, notwithstanding the special taxes imposed for revenue purposes at the last session of Parliament, which the Minister of Finance, when he announced them in his Budget of last September, expected would realize $7,000,000 during the six months of the current fiscal year then ensuing. That is to say, our shortage as between actual expenditure and actual revenue, based upon the tariff taxation as it was a year ago, was not $60,000,000 but $67,000,000. \ye have taken $7,000,000 more out of the pockets of the people of this country during the current six months than would have been taken out unaer the system of taxation that prevailed before the short summer session.
Again, I find that, notwithstanding this increase of taxation, expecting a further increase of the debt during the coming year to the amount of another $60,000,000, exclusive of war expenditure, the Minister of Finance brings in additional taxation which he hopes will yield $30,000,000. But besides that special taxation, which he proposes by his Budget just brought down, is the $14,000,000 of extra taxation which will accrue because of his Budget proposals of September last. We are carrying, then, a load of extra taxation, as the result of the Budget of last September and the present Budget, of not $30,000,000, but $44,000,000. The load of taxation has been increased for the year which we are about to enter upon to the amount of $44,000,000, and we shall still have a difference between revenue and expenditure, on the estimates of my hon. friend, of $30,000,000. Therefore we are $74,000,000 behind in our business transactions as expected for the coming year, aside altogether from war expenditure, according to the statements made by the Minister of Finance. That is a sufficiently startling condition to warrant the statement I have already made, namely, that the 'Government scarcely seem to have appreciated the gravity of the situation. Although our revenues have fallen so tremendously even in the face of such enormous increased taxation, we still are unahle to meet the requirements of the public service, according to the estimates of my hon. friend.
The Government of to-day may have some means of creating something out of nothing, of creating money otherwise

than by getting it from the people by way of taxes. But, unless they have some other means of securing money, they are taking the position that they are not called upon under present circumstances to do what every other person, corporation, government, or other organization throughout the world has to do, that is, to bring its expenditures into some comparison with its revenues, present or prospective. As I read the Estimates, as I have followed the Budget statement, the Government have absolutely ignored -that as being a necessity. If I have read correctly the Budget statement of the hon, Minister of Finance, he proposes to make the same expenditure on current account and on capital account during the coming year, and to face the shortage of which he speaks, as he did during the present year, when he had no such reason to expect a shortage, and had not found it necessary to impose an enormous additional burden of taxation upon the Canadian people in order to bring his revenue even approximately up to his (expenditure. I do not wish to labour the point unduly, but surely it is the business of those charged with the administration of the affairs of our country to keep some reasonable balance between revenue and expenditure without adding repeatedly and seriously to the burdens borne by the people. If the Government are going to take the view that expenditures may be made freely, liberally, and carelessly, and that the result is simply an increase in some measure of the burden of taxation, and that this burden is something that really makes no *serious difference to the people, I can only say that I do not think they appreciate the *seriousness of the situation or (the means that should be taken to remedy it.
I do not wish to deal with the question of the war or the war expenditures at any great length; but it appears to me that, if the Government has failed in its appreciation of the gravity of the financial situation of the country as it stands at present, it has failed even more seriously in regard to the gravity of the situation so far as the great world-war now in progress is concerned. The Government has a duty besides that of collecting taxes and spending money. It has a duty to give inspiration and direction td the minds of the people of the country in regard to all great questions that may come up for consideration, and ten times more so in a case such as that which confronts Canada, the Empire and the world at the present time. I do not wish to be misunderstood as to my
[Mr. Oliver.}
conception of the position of the Government of Canada. The Government of Canada is hot responsible for the occurrence of this war, or for its direction. The responsibility of the Government of Canada is that Canada shall take her proper part, with her men and with her means, in supporting the cause with which the interests of Canada are absolutely bound up: the maintenance of the prestige of the British Empire and the preservation of human liberty throughout the world.
The existence of the war has been used, it appears to me, as an excuse for a great many actions on the " part of the Government and for a great many omissions on the part of the Government for which there is no excuse. As I have said, this Government neither directs the war nor is responsible for it, but this Government is responsible for the part that the Canadian people take in the war; and it is there, it seems to me, where they have failed in discharging their responsibilities; failed at any rate in appreciating the measure of their responsibility in the Budget proposals that they have laid before the House.
In the Budget proposals of last summer, the Finance Minister announced the necessity of a war loan of $50,000,000. We have been informed since this session opened that $50,000,000 will keep practically 50,000 men in the field for six months. We are proposing another war loan of $100,000,000 to last, I presume, for a year, and, if I understood the Prime Minister correctly, his statement was that we were to have 90,000 or possibly 100,000 men in the field. If 50,000 men require $50,000,000 to maintain them for six months, certainly $100,000,000 will not maintain 100,000 men for a year at the same rate. I do not wish to press this point; it is a question that is eminently for the responsibility of the Government, but the facts and figures are as I have stated. Do they believe that they can keep 100,000 men in the field for twelve months on an appropriation of $100,000,000, and is 100,000 men the limit of their intention in regard to the aid that they are to give the Empire during this war? We do not know how long this war may last;, we do not know what turn it may take; we only know what our duty is and what results we desire to see achieved. At such a time, if ever, our resources should be conserved so that the money can be found and the men oan be put in the field and kept there as long as the necessity remains. This is not

a time to dismiss lightly with a wave of the hand the question of expenditures, of deficits, of revenue or lack of revenue. This is the time above all others when every care should be taken, when every dollar should be conserved, when every portion of the credit of the country should be maintained to the highest degree as long as it can be so maintained. What is the use of our saying that we are in this war to a finish with our last man and our last dollar when we are throwing money right and left on this, that or the other expenditure, connected with the well-being of this country, it may be, but still not necessary in any degree for the maintenance of Canada's position in connection with the war? We are liberal with our money; the money that we spend in military support we borrow in England, and we go to England also to borrow the money that we spend over and above our revenues for the very .ordinary current expenses of the country.
In following the remarks of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. A. C. Mac-donell), I noted that he made a strong point of the commitments of the late Government with regard to large public expenditures of various kinds, and especially with regard to railway expenditure, and gave these commitments of the late Government as a reason for the large expenditures at the present time of the present Government. I will not go into that matter at any great length, except to say in regard to one of the great commitments of the late Government, namely, the Transcontinental railway, that,
[DOT] if my memory is correct, when the late Government went out of power that railway was within fifteen per cent of being completed. That was three and a half years ago. I do not know how long it is taking this Government to complete that fifteen per cent, or how much money they are spending on it, but if they are using the same energy and the same economy that their predecessors used, certainly that expenditure should have been off the slate before now. In regard to the Canadian Northern, my hon. friend told of the guarantees by the Federal Government and of guarantees by the Provincial governments, and said that the enormous cash bonus paid by this Government was necessary in order to protect the guarantees already given by the Federal and Provincial governments. The cash subsidy paid by this Government to the Canadian Northern railway had practically no bearing on the security for the guarantees given by either the Federal
Government or the provinces. The Canadian Northern railway was a sufficiently completed system, upon the guarantees given by the Federal Government and the provinces; and the grant of money by this Government was of their own motion, of their own desire to, as I presume, gratify the ambitions of the projectors of the Canadian Northern railway, but with absolutely no justification from a financial point of view, as the conditions are at the present time. They must take the whole responsibility for the vast expenditure of cash that they have made in regard to the Canadian Northern railway for that part of its line which runs through the province of British Columbia. The late Government was not responsible in any particular, in any degree, for a dollar of that expenditure either directly or indirectly, by reason of commitments, obligations or for any other reason.
I desire to draw the attention of the House more particularly to the means that is proposed by the Finance Minister to raise increased revenue. We will admit that if he keeps up his expenditure he must have revenue, he must have money, and he must get it either by increased taxes or by increased borrowings. As to what proportion should be increased taxes and what proportion should be borrowings I shall not argue, that is not the point I wish to bring forward. I wish to say that, assuming the necessity for increasing the taxes, I for one am glad to see this Government adopt the principle of direct taxation. I do not say that the details are in all particulars as I would like to see them, but it is certainly an important point that a Government whose policy is tariff for protection should, at this time of stress and serious conditions, adopt the principle of direct taxation as a means of raising revenue and of meeting a deficit. It is, in the first place, a square, straight admission that their tariff is a tariff for protection and not for revenue. If an increase of tariff would give increase of revenue now was the time to make that increase of tariff if it was revenue the Government wanted. We maintain that it is a fact that undue increase, of tariff will not give revenue, and the direct taxation features of the Budget are an absolute admission of that contention.

Has the hon. gentleman not just argued that the increase in duties which we made last year had produced some $7,000,000 more revenue than

would have been obtained if we had not increased them?
Yes.
Now he is arguing that an increase does not give more revenue at all.

No, my hon. friend is
mistaken. I say that if the Government wanted to raise $30,000,000 at this session, being a Government whose policy is a policy of protection by tariff, if they believed that any increase of tariff would raise that $30,000,060, now was the time to show their faith by their works. But they knew that no possible increase that they could make in the tariff would give them that amount of revenue and therefore they did not take that means of raising the additional revenue, they adopted the system of direct taxation as a means of raising revenue while they did increase the measure of protection already in force. I do not know how far this will be acceptable to the people of the country. I am inclined to think that there are many people who would have accepted a higher tariff for purposes of revenue, but that there are very few of the general body of consumers who will accept the higher tariff for purposes of protection and at the same time direct taxes in order to raise revenue.
How much revenue is expected to be raised by these two means of taxation? I understood the Finance Minister to say that he expected $30,000,000, of which he expected to get from $8,000,000 to $10,000,000 by direct taxation and. the balance of $20,000,000 or $22,000,000 by indirect or protective duties. The Toronto Star has gone into -[DOT]-the matter somewhat and figures that, on the business of last year, the direct taxes proposed by the Budget, exclusive of the Patent Medicines tax would produce $14,000,000, and I cannot imagine that the Finance Minister had not those figures at hand when he framed the Bud.'fi he had in mind receiving a larger proportion of revenue from the direct tax side of his Budget than he gave the House to understand. His hopes of revenue centered rather on the direct taxes than on the indirect taxes. With regard to the direct taxes let me point this out. We all agree that there must be taxation, there must be revenue, and the whole question as between one party and the other, and between any two individuals in arguing upon taxation, is in regard to the fairness of the taxation. If the taxation is equally levied according to the ability of the different

people to carry it, then it is carried easily and without detriment to the country. But if it is levied unequally, if the man of small means and great responsibility is compelled to carry more than his share and the man of greater means and less responsibilities carries less than his share, then there is an undue burden resting upon one section of the community, and, as a consequence, the whole community is hampered in its progress. In the scheme of direct taxation that the minister proposes I find that of $14,000,000 the banks will contribute $1,000,000, and the trust companies $1,000,000.
Are you against that?

Not at all. Then $300,000 is expected on insurance premiums, $7,000,000 from increased postal rates, and $3,000,000 from railway passengers. It appears to me that the ordinary man who uses the postal facilities is bearing an unduly heavy share of this burden of taxation, wh'ile the great financial interests are bearing an unduly light proportion. Furthermore, I do not agree with the Finance Minister that it was not advisable to levy an income tax. I do not know where he would go for money except where money is. The burden should be levied according to the ability of the people to bear it. The burden should be laid equally, but the minister is not doing that when the banks with their great resources and profits pay only $1,000,000, and the trust companies with their profits only $1,000,000, while the ordinary people who write letters pay $7,000,000, and the people vrho ride in railway trains pay $3,000,000. The principle of direct taxation is sound, but the principle must be carried out in a sound way. The advantage of direct taxation is that the tax can be levied according to the ability of the person to bear it. When the tax is not so levied, when it is levied lightly on the wealthy and heavily on those who are not wealthy, it has many of the disadvantageous features of the ordinary protective tariff.
Do not the banks and the trust companies post letters?

They will help to pay that tax, of course. But does not my hon. friend think that the banks, with their hundreds of millions of free circulation and the advantages they have at the hands of the Government of Canada, might fairly be asked to pay a larger share than they are being asked to do?
My hon. friend said that the stamp tax would fall entirely on the poor people.

Oh, no, I said the poor
people would pay the greater part of it.
Oh, no.
Give us the figures.
I have not got them.
If my hon. friend had taken the trouble to get them, he would have found that he was far from the facts.
I do not think my hon. friend could get those figures.
We will try.

The side of the Budget
proposals that calls for the most attention, and will probably receive the greatest attention at the hands of the people, is the proposals relating to tariff increases. It was quite in order that my hon. friend from South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) should be the member on the Government side of the House to follow my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean), and defend this high tariff Budget. As I read it, the tariff was made for Toronto, by Toronto and in Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was made in Canada for Canadians.

But only for some of the Canadians, very few in fact. We are anxious to see a tariff framed for all Canadians, just as we should be glad to see a system of taxation that would lay the burden equally on the shoulders of all of us. The proposal to increase by 5 per cent the duty on goods coming from Great Britain, and by 7i per cent on goods coming from other countries, is, in fact, an increase in the tariff of 25 per cent. By a stroke of the pen the Finance Minister or the Government of this country have raised the tariff by one-fourth. They have made the tariff of Canada to-day higher in many particulars than the so-called National Policy of 1878, which was reduced in many particulars by those who framed it after they had had experience of it for 16 years. By the introduction of this Budget, the Finance Minister has taken away in important instances the advantages that were given to this country by the tariff reductions of 1904.
There were no reductions then.	*
That is a great point. They need points badly.

The Finance Minister said that this was a tariff for Canadians. I
notice that some Canadians will do very well out of it. I see our old friend the lumber combine figures quite successfully in this tariff. Lumber dressed on one side only was made free under tne tariff of 1894 as a concession to the special conditions existing at that time in the prairie regions of Canada. It has been recognized as being an important benefit to the people of that western country. There have repeatedly been demands made upon the late Government and this Government to have that condition of free lumber removed. My hon. friend has removed it, and to-day that lumber stands under a duty of seven and one-half per cent.
That is a war tax.

We will deal with that
lat^r. Lumber that costs $15 a thousand and was free, now pays $1.12$ a thousand duty. Lumber that costs $20 a thousand which formerly paid $5, now pays $6.50, and lumber that costs $25 a thousand formerly paid $6.25, now pays $8.25. If there is one institution or organization in the Dominion of Canada that did not merit consideration at the hands of this Government it was the lumber combine. My hon. friend has seen fit to place a taxation that is unjustified, unwarranted from	any point of
view upon the people of western Canada who depend	largely upon
imported lumber. While my hon. friend is preaching a campaign of patriotism and production, while' the Minister of Agriculture is lecturing, and sending lecturers, throughout the West enjoining the farmers on the prairies to raise stock, to go into cattle and hogs, which must have shelter in buildings made of lumber or they cannot live, the Minister of Finance puts a bar of from $1 to $1.50 a thousand upon the use of that lumber for the benefit of an industry and an organization that, I say, has no claim upon the consideration of this Government or of the people of this country from any point of view. Just how far the lumber combine will benefit by this duty I cannot say, but I find that during last year we imported lumber to the value of $4,428,000 and that on that amount the revenue to the country will be $221,000.
How much of that lumber came in free?
It all came in free.
It would affect the calculation if some of this were free and some dutiable.

The Trade and Commerce returns show that in the year ended March 31,	1914, we imported free of
duty $4,428,341 worth of lumber, upon which, with the duty now imposed, the consumer would pay, or the treasury would receive $221,000. But while we iim ported four and a half millions worth we exported nearly twenty million dollars worth showing that we are not dependent on imports for our supply of lumber. As a matter of fact, I fancy, for every thousand feet of lumber we import, we consume twice as much as we import, and if we do, then, as a result of the imposition of this 7i per cent duty, while we will pay the treasury $221,000, we will pay the gentlemen who constitute the British Columbia lumber combine $442,000. The duty of 71 per cent will cost the settler in the Northwest, on this calculation, not $221,000 but
10 p.m. $663,000 in addition to what he has been paying in the past. That is one of my hon. friend's contributions to the campaign of patriotism and production.
Now, take cement. We imported-709,000 cwt. in the year I have mentioned of a value of $332,564 and the duty collected amounted to $69,684. On that amount of cement there will be $24,279 of additional duty under the increased tariff. In other words, the cement combine, these good Canadians, these true patriots, these gentlemen who are out for patriotism and production, get the benefit of a 30 per cent additional protection at the hands of my hon. friend. And the consumer of cement pays $24,000 in addition? No, he pays on whatever amount of cement is used in Canada that is purchased in Canada as well as on the amount that is imported. I do not imagine that we import one-quarter of the cement that we use.
One-tenth.

If we import only onetenth of what we use, then this little increase in the tariff, instead of costing $24,000 additional, will cost $240,000 to the consumer of cement. Again a boost for the campaign of patriotism and production!

We know that cement
was reduced a few years ago-I think it was two years ago-and that in practical operation the foreign manufacturers of cement put half of the reduction in their own pockets and the consumers did not benefit to the extent the hon. gentleman is setting forth.

I do not know anything
about that, but I think I can demonstrate that the producers of cement will benefit to the amount I say by the change which has been made in the tariff and I do not think that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance will question that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Oh, yes, I will.
No one will agree with you oil that.

However, that is a matter the facts will demonstrate, and there is no doubt about it the consumer will have to pay. I notice that this Budget provides that mowers and reapers and binder twine are not subject to this increase of 7J per cent. That is an important omission. It is of great advantage to the people of Western Canada particularly, and to the farmers of all Canada, that mowers and reapers are not subject to this increased duty, but mowers and reapers are not the only implements that are necessary to carry on this campaign of production and patriotism.
Ask them why they were left off the list of articles subject to increased taxation.

I wonder why they happen to be left out of the list of articles subject to the increased taxation, unless the increase was liable to raise their price. Some of the gentleihen on the other side can answer that question at their leisure, I will not press for an answer at the moment. While mowers and reapers are exempt from this increase of duty, there is a long list of other agricultural implements that are not exempt, and which might be, such as engines, threshers, ploughs, harrows, drills, seeders, rollers, packers, hay-rakes, potato-diggers. The plough, as everybody knows, is the symbol of agriculture; it is the fundamental implement of agriculture, and the plough pays an increased duty of seven and a half per cent. We imported in the year ending 1914, one million dollars' worth of ploughs and the duty on them was two hundred thousand dollars. If we import one million dollars' worth of ploughs next year they will pay $275,000 duty, which means that the campaign of patriotism and production will be aided by levying an additional tax of $75,000 upon the men who buy the ploughs.

That is the way the
farmers are made prosperous.

Yes. In this country I do not think that we import the larger pro-

portion of our ploughs. We have men in Canada who make ploughs; they are very excellent ploughs, and they are made in such numbers and of such quality that they are even exported to the United States to compete in the United States markets with the product of that country. So that, if we import one million dollars' worth of ploughs, we may reasonably believe that we produce three million dollars' worth in this country. And so our bill in respect to ploughs, under the seven and a half per cent increase, will be not $75,000 but $225,000, $75,000 of which will go to the Treasury, and the balance to the patriotic manufacturers of ploughs to aid in the campaign of patriotism and production.
I hope the House will pardon me for taking so much time on this feature of the case, but my hon. friend from Toronto was so insistent on the point that everybody was satisfied with this tariff, that I am sure hon. gentlemen will permit me to show to what extent we have reason to be satisfied with it. But there , are people besides farmers who are interested in this tariff, because many of the people of Canada use cottons and woollens. In the year ending 31st March, 1914, under eight particular items, we imported woollens to the value of over twenty million dollars, blankets, worsteds, tweeds, etc., and upon that importation we paid a duty of five and a half million dollars, if we buy that same quantity of woollens next year, then under the five per cent and seven and a half per cent increase we will pay in the neighbourhood of $1,225,000 additional to what we paid before. Remember we do not get all these goods from Great Britain and they do not all come under the preference, although the larger portion does. In cottons, taking four items, we imported seven million dollars' worth last year, and we paid on that $1,225,000 duty. Averaging the five per cent and the seven and a half per cent increase, we will pay in addition $409,000 on the same importation next year. I do not imagine that we import one-half the cottons we use in Canada. We have immense cotton factories, we must be producing a great deal of cotton goods, and I think we produce at least twice as much as we import, so that while the Minister of Finance takes less than half a million dollars out of the people for the Treasury, his friends, these good Canadians, these patriotic manufacturers of cotton, will draw down anywhere from one million to one and a half million dollars. There 25
is no doubt they are highly satisfied with the increase in the tariff. There is another class of patriots in this country who ought to have attention at this particular time,
I speak of the manufacturers of boots. In the year ending 1914 we purchased $4,225,000 worth of boots and we paid $1,225,000 duty upon these boots. Taking the increase at seven per cent, because the larger portion of these boots comes from the United States, we will he paying $300,000 more duty upon the same quantity of boots imported next year. But everybody knows that we only import a comparatively small part of the boots we use in this country. I fancy that we make at any rate three pairs of boots in Canada for home use for every pair that we import. If that fact is a fact-and it is unquestionably a fact in this time of strife and hardship, when the cost of living has gone up and the means of living have gone down-my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, by his Budget, is handing to the manufacturers of boots in Canada approximately $1,000,000 a year.

What does the hon.
member for St. Antoine (Mr. Ames) think of that?
Perhaps the hon. gentleman, while he is on the subject, will say why this Government raised the duty on boots by five per cent?
My hon. friend will have all he can handle in explaining what his Government has done. The point is what his Government has done, not what the late Government did.

It is you I am asking
for an explanation. I hope you will make it. [DOT]
My hon. friend is asking for an explanation of something that is not pertinent to the subject. We are discussing war taxes that are being imposed at the present time.
So-called war taxes.

Yes. My conclusion is
that, if the estimate of the amount of home production is correct, to those sterling patriots who are producing boots in Canada so greatly to the credit of Canada, and who are so strongly upholding Canada in its share of this war that is in progress, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has handed out a little matter of $1,000,000 at this time, when every man is wondering where his revenue is to come from and how



he can make his expenditure and his revenue meet.
That is the way the bootmakers die for the flag.

In the exposure that we
have had lately, if there is any class of manufacturers in this country who are not entitled to special consideration at the hands of this Government, it is our friends Who make boots.

Who make boots for
the army. There are some very good makers of boots at St. John.

Who make boots for the
army. My hon. friends have spoken of this Budget as a war Budget. It is a war Budget inasmuch as it is a Budget that is placed before the country while a war is in progress, but it is not a Budget which provides for meeting the expenses of that war. That we have on the authority of the Minister of Finance, and the facts are evident on the face of the record. The war is responsible for many things; but it is not responsible for the mismanagement of the finances of Canada which has occurred since our friends have taken office, and which has resulted in a deficit as between current revenue and current expenditure for the current year, amounting, on the authority of the Minister of Finance, to, I think, $20,000,000. .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
$10,000,000 this year, and that is with an additional and special tax, which is expected to produce $7,000,000 during the last six months of the year, so that it really amounts to a deficit of $17,000,000 on current account.
I would like to see the Government appreciate their responsibility in regard to the part that Canada has to take in this war. They have not done so up to date; and it is not right or fair-I will not go further and say what ought to be said-that the Government should make the pretence, should hold out the false signal, and declare that the existence of this war is a reason why they increase the burdens on the people of Canada for the benefit of their particular friends. We hear a great deal in war time	vessels sailing under false ,
flags. When this Government put forward, as tneir excuse for increasing tne tax burden upon the people of this country, the existence of the war in Europe, tney are sailing under a false flag; they are attempting to

trade upon the patriotism of the people for the benefit of their particular friends and supporters, the manufacturing interests. This is neither a time nor an occasion when any government of any British country siiould come before Parliament and the people with such a proposal. This is a time when we ought to have fair play, fair dealing, and square talking. The Government should not attempt to mislead public opinion by mis-stating the facts of the case, putting upon their stamp, " war tax," when not a particle nor a fraction of the cost of the stamp is intended to pay any part of the war cost.
What about the interest?
We are not even paying the interest.
Oh, yes.

Accorumg to the statement of the Minister of Finance, we are not even providing enough money to pay the expenditures that we have undertaken, aside altogether from the war, let alone interest. We have to borrow money to pay the interest, as my hon. friend knows.
Nonsense.

Patriotism and production ! The words sound well, and there is no doubt that there is great need in Canada at the present time both of patriotism and of proauction. Why is it that our friends are holding meetings here and there throughout the country and urging upon the farmers in the West to increase their acreage, to increase their production, for the sake of patriotism? Do they know why the farmers in the West have not increased their acreage during the past few years? Do they know that the acreage of production in the West in 1914 was no greater than it was in 1911, and do they know why?
Yes.
Does my hon. friend know why?

Economically the
world can consume only a certain quantity of food, and if you increase production, as some hon. gentlemen furiously profess they intend to do in the West, you will only heap waste on the market. While you may interchange manufactures and have five pianos or five motor cars or five anything else you like instead of one, you cannot eat any more than you did before, no matter what you may do.

In 1914 the area of production in the West was no greater than it was in 1911, and to-day the Government and the people who claim to have leadership in Canada are urging upon the people of the West to increase their production. Do our friends recall the conditions that existed throughout the prairie provinces immediately after they took office in 1911? Do they remember the tremendous crop that was on the ground, the unfavourable weather conditions that existed, the grain blockade that took place, the rotting of the grain in the stooks and in the granaries? Do they remember what was done when pressure was exerted in this House to secure an outlet for this grain by means of reduced railway rates and by means of tariff concessions in respect of trade with the United States? When it was too late, railway rates were reduced, but no tariff concessions were made. Railway rates were reduced for grain that was routed through, but not for grain that was sold in the States subject to the tariff; it had to pay the higher rates. Well, I can assure my hon. friend that when a farmer has seen his crop rot on the ground or in the granary, and when he has not the wherewithal to seed that ground the next year, he is just in the same position as any business man would be. In the first place, he is discouraged; in the second place, he cannot go on. And when the next year prices were abnormally low; when oats were selling in the province of Alberta at 15, 16, and 18 cents a bushel, what was done by this Government to relieve the situation? Anything? Nothing, absolutely. Since that time the changes in the United States tariff have given an advantage to Canadian producers. There has been a reduction in the duty on oats, and last year the reduction of the United States duty to 6 cents a bushel enabled the people of the western country to dispose of their oats, I shall not say at a living price, but they were able to get rid of them, and they would not have been able to do so otherwise. Yet my hon. friends wonder why production stands still. They think that by issuing pamphlets and by holding meetings in board rooms of banks they can instruct the farmer how to increase production. If they would give the farmer the benefit of a market, then he would increase production. At the present time, owing to the war, he has a market. Give him reasonable accommodation at the bank and you shall not need to issue pamphlets or hold lectures; he will increase the production all right enough. But he has to have 25i
the money. Unless you are prepared to let him have the money, he cannot make the production. If these kings of finance, who are so wise on every subject after everything is over, would make their arrangements so that they could and would finance the farmers of the western country during this year of high prices, I will guarantee that they will increase production. But talk will not do it, and the levying of extra taxes will not do it. The 25-cent increase that is proposed to be placed in the tariff by this present .Budget is a campaign against patriotism and against production, and it will take years and great effort-on the part, I am sure, of some other government than this-to overcome the loss that the country-will sustain by reason of its impos^on.
